new_statements.relation_note: Introduction gives PA consonant/vowel inventory and the t/r/n-dialect diagnostics (Powhatan-centred); the word-list repeatedly comments on what the written accents in the 1585-88 recordings represent (pitch vs stress accent), as quoted.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Not a rule for the language: Geary interprets the acute accent marks that Hariot/White wrote on some 1585-88 Carolina Algonquian words. Reading them through Fox (Meskwaki) prosody, he takes most of them to mark a high pitch accent on the syllable that was the Proto-Algonquian antepenult (= the penult of the attested, apocopated form), followed by a falling accent on the old penult (attested ultima); for other words he says the mark sits 'where there should be a stress-accent'. His global classification: Hariot's accents are pitch-accents, not stress-accents. Word-level prominence itself is never described first-hand; no speaker was ever heard by a linguist.
new_statements.exceptions: Geary himself flags words where the written accent 'does not correspond with stress' (the Towhee name, scanned 'Chiwheeo') and words where it 'is a stress-accent, not a pitch accent' (the berry and nut names, scanned 'Sacquentimmener', 'Sagatémener'; also the ?Vireo name, scanned 'Iachdwanjes': 'the accent seems to indicate stress'); for the place-name Occam he says accent placement cannot be determined.
new_statements.identity_note: Appendix devoted to the words recorded 1584-90 by Hariot, White and compilation among the Roanoke/Secotan/Croatoan-area tribes, which Quinn and Geary label 'Carolina Algonkian [Car. Alg.]' as opposed to 'Virginia Algonquian'; Geary's introduction (part A) is mostly about Powhatan/Strachey, but part B (word-list, pp. 884-900) treats the Carolina forms one by one. Same corpus as Glottolog's Glottolog's most extensive description (Hariot-White-compilation). Lawson's 1709 Pamlico list is not treated.

About 54 words/phrases carry respelled pronunciations in brackets with one syllable capitalized in 50 of them (e.g. Nitáp [knee-TAUP] 'my friend', Winkapew [wing-KAH-poe] 'good person', Runapewak [duh-nah-PAY-wahk] 'the people', Pumitukew [PUHM-tuh-koh] 'river', Mahkusun [mah-KUH-sun] 'shoes') and acute accents on some orthographic forms (Yapám, Anáskimin, Pakán); the marked syllable varies (final, penult, antepenult, initial). These are stress MARKS on reconstructed forms (wordlist-style data), not a statement of a rule, and reflect Rudes's reconstitution…

sources.citation: Coastal Carolina Indian Center. n.d. [c. 2006]. The Algonquian Language Reborn: An Interview with Blair Rudes. Coastal Carolina Indian Center (Blair A. Rudes Indigenous Language Collection). Web page.
sources.note: No stress/tone content. Relevant identity claim only: 'The Algonquian spoken in the towns around Albemarle and Pamlico sounds was quite similar to the Algonquian spoken in Virginia. In fact, it is fair to say that they were dialects of the same language.. Briefly, the pronunciation of Carolina and Virginia Algonquian was essentially the same.' This would make Powhatan reconstitutions (Siebert 1975, already read and silent on stress) the nearest proxy; it is not itself a description.
